items.prompt: How confident are you that you could make your team's plan visible to everyone?
Which version of the plan can your team actually use?

options.label: A shared list with names and dates
A plan you remember and explain when asked
A rough feeling about who is busy

items.explanation: Names and dates let anyone spot a gap and offer help, while a plan kept in your head only works while you are present.

items.prompt: Write your team's current plan as a short shared list with who does what and by when.

criteria: Assigns each task to a named person with a date
Puts the list somewhere the whole team can see it

items.prompt: In your own words, explain why a plan kept only in your head is hard for a team to use.

criteria: Explains that others cannot see or act on an unseen plan
Notes that a shared plan lets anyone spot gaps

items.prompt: How confident are you that you could ask for help before a deadline instead of after it?
You realize on Monday that one part of the project is behind. What is the most useful move?

options.label: Tell the team what is behind and ask for help now
Stay quiet and try to catch up alone
Wait until Friday to see if it works out

items.explanation: Flagging it early turns a problem into a plan, while waiting turns it into an emergency.

items.prompt: Name one task you are behind on and write the exact sentence you would use to ask a teammate for help today.

criteria: Identifies a specific task that is behind
Writes a clear, direct request for help

items.prompt: In your own words, explain why asking for help early is planning rather than failing.

criteria: Explains that early requests give the team time to respond
Contrasts early asking with a last-minute emergency
